article.overview: An infrared imager is an instrument class defined by the part of the spectrum it observes, not by one design. Infrared radiation carries two different kinds of signal from the Moon: sunlight reflected by the surface at near- and shortwave infrared wavelengths, and heat emitted by the surface at thermal infrared wavelengths. An infrared imager may record one or both. This article covers the generic class and four examples that are documented to different depths: the Apollo 17 Infrared Scanning Radiometer, which mapped lunar surface thermal emission from lunar orbit [8][9]; the Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, a nine-channel thermal radiometer whose data acquisition is reported as ongoing [1][2][3][4]; the Lunar Thermal Mapper on Lunar Trailblazer, which launched in 2025 but whose mission ended before science operations were reported [11][12]; and the Imaging Infrared Spectrometer on Chandrayaan-2 [10]. Band-specific detail belongs to other entries. Shortwave infrared is covered in 041 (Shortwave infrared camera), longwave infrared in 042 (Longwave infrared camera), thermal imaging cameras in 038 (Thermal imaging camera), and multi-band spectral mapping in 035 (Hyperspectral imager). This article does not repeat those entries in full.
article.description: An infrared imager forms an image or map from infrared radiation, which has wavelengths longer than visible light. Its detectors respond either to sunlight reflected from the surface or to heat emitted by the surface, depending on the band. In thermal infrared work the measured quantity is the radiance, the amount of emitted energy that reaches the instrument in each spectral band. Converting radiance into surface temperature requires an estimate of emissivity, the efficiency with which a surface radiates, which depends on composition and texture. For this reason multi-band radiometers record several channels, so that temperature and spectral emission features can be separated. Infrared imagers take two broad forms. Broadband radiometers produce temperature or brightness maps from a small number of wide channels. Imaging spectrometers record many narrow, contiguous bands and are used for mineral and volatile mapping. The boundary between them is not sharp. This article places spectrometers only where they are needed to define the class; their detailed treatment belongs to 035.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The examples in this article point to three related purposes. Thermal mapping. Diviner is described as mapping the thermal state of the Moon and its diurnal and seasonal variability [1]. The Apollo 17 Infrared Scanning Radiometer was designed to map thermal emission from the lunar surface and to measure nighttime temperatures that are difficult to obtain from Earth-based telescopes [9]. Mineralogy. Diviner's three channels near 8 µm are used to map the wavelength of the Christiansen feature, a spectral signature used to classify regolith mineralogy [2][3]. Composition and water. ISRO describes the Chandrayaan-2 IIRS as intended to map mineral and volatile composition [10]. The Lunar Thermal Mapper was intended to measure surface temperature and the minerals that make up the surface, to help confirm the presence and location of water, working alongside the HVM3 spectrometer [11][12]. The applications described in the sources therefore include global thermal state, regolith composition and volatile studies. The Diviner team's paper also lists cold traps among its subjects [1]. Its full text was not read for this article, so no quantitative cold-trap result is taken from it.
article.operating_principle: An infrared imager converts infrared radiation into an electrical signal in each spectral band. A filter or grating selects the band, and a detector array records the signal. In a thermal radiometer, a calibrated detector views the surface; the signal is converted to radiance and then to brightness temperature. Diviner uses a linear 21-element thermopile detector array for each channel, with a focal-plane bandpass filter setting each channel's spectral response [2][3]. Its two telescopes are boresighted [3]. Mapping is pushbroom nadir: the instrument records readings line by line as the spacecraft moves, with periodic space, blackbody and solar calibrations [3]. The Apollo 17 Infrared Scanning Radiometer is described as measuring thermal emission from the lunar surface from the service module in lunar orbit [9]. ISRO describes IIRS as measuring reflected solar radiation in 256 contiguous bands between about 0.8 and 5.0 µm [10]. eoPortal gives the LTM's channel structure as 11 bands within 7–10 µm and four bands spanning 6–100 µm [11].
article.scientific_importance: Thermal infrared observations record how the lunar surface heats and cools through the lunar day and across seasons. Surface temperature controls which volatile materials can persist in cold, shadowed regions, so temperature maps are a basic input to water and volatile studies [1][3]. Orbital thermal mapping also gives global coverage that a surface instrument cannot provide. Diviner's published coverage statements for one year of mapping include nighttime coverage of more than 75% of the Moon at the equator and 100% poleward of 70 degrees [3]. The Apollo 17 Infrared Scanning Radiometer showed that orbital thermal mapping of the surface was feasible and reported about 10^8 independent temperature measurements [9]. Its preliminary results placed the strongest thermal anomalies in Oceanus Procellarum, with relatively few on the far side and some cold spots [9]. These are preliminary findings as the source describes them and have not been checked here against later publications.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an infrared imager. The four examples differ in mission, spectral range, detector design and status, so each value below is tied to a named instrument and source. Where a source does not publish a value, the text says "not publicly specified". Mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the accessed sources for the Apollo 17 ISR, Diviner or IIRS, and the LTM mass and power are also not stated. The examples are not directly comparable and should not be ranked.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not publicly specified for any of the four examples in the sources accessed. Diviner's structure is described qualitatively as an optics bench, an elevation/azimuth yoke and an instrument mount, without measurements [2].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for the Apollo 17 ISR, Diviner or IIRS in the sources accessed. eoPortal gives a combined mass of 20 kg for the LTM and HVM3 payloads, with no per-instrument figure [11]. The 200 kg figure on the Oxford page is for the whole Lunar Trailblazer spacecraft, not for the payload [12].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for any of the four examples in the sources accessed. Neither the Diviner SIS nor the UCLA instrument page states power [2][3]. A power statement would require electrical interface documents that were not accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Infrared imagers on the Moon operate in vacuum, under large diurnal temperature swings and in a radiation environment. Thermal radiometers measure surface emission both by day and by night. Diviner's coverage statements include nighttime mapping [3], and the Apollo 17 ISR was designed specifically to measure nighttime temperatures [9]. Calibration is an operational requirement. Diviner performs periodic space, blackbody and solar calibrations during mapping [3]. Radiometric accuracy also depends on known viewing geometry, including local time and emission angle; the Apollo 17 ISR reports an absolute accuracy of 2 K [9]. Detector cooling, thermal set-points and radiation tolerances are not stated for any of the four examples in the sources accessed, so none is given. Data gaps are also an operational issue: PDS reports missing brightness-temperature values for much of Diviner's solar-channel data since April 2019 and attributes them to processing errors rather than an instrument fault [4].
article.limitations: Brightness temperature is not surface temperature. Converting a radiometer's measured radiance to a surface temperature needs an assumed or measured emissivity, and the result depends on surface roughness and viewing geometry. Resolution figures are not comparable across examples. The Apollo 17 ISR reports about 2.2 km at nadir [9]; Diviner reports an instantaneous field of view of approximately 179 × 307 m at 50 km altitude [3]; ISRO gives about 80 m for IIRS at a 3.0 µm objective [10]; eoPortal gives 25 m per pixel for the LTM [11]. These figures belong to different instruments, altitudes and products. Diviner's data products have a documented gap in solar-channel brightness temperatures since April 2019 [4]. The Apollo 17 ISR results are preliminary in the source [9]. The LTM's science return is not verified, and the IIRS operating status is not stated on the ISRO page [10][11]. Orbital infrared imagers provide maps from altitude and do not measure a single point on the surface in situ.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All four examples are orbital or cislunar instruments. The sources accessed describe the Apollo 17 ISR as flown on the service module of the Apollo 17 spacecraft [9], Diviner as integrated onto LRO [6][7], the LTM as a payload of Lunar Trailblazer [11], and IIRS as a Chandrayaan-2 orbiter payload [10]. None is described in these sources as a surface payload. A surface infrared imager would need lander interfaces that are not specified here, and none is asserted.
transportation_process: Integrate the radiometer or imager into the spacecraft's payload on Earth. For Diviner, NASA/JPL photographs show the instrument prepared for thermal balance testing and then following integration to LRO [6][7].
Test the payload before flight. A NASA/JPL photograph shows final preparations for Diviner's thermal balance testing at JPL [6]; the test results are not stated in the sources accessed.
Launch the spacecraft. LRO launched on 18 June 2009 [5]; Lunar Trailblazer launched on 27 February 2025 (UTC) as a rideshare with IM-2 [11].
Transfer to the Moon and insert into lunar orbit. For Lunar Trailblazer, the sources accessed record the mission as ended on 31 July 2025 and do not confirm lunar orbit insertion [11].
Commission the instrument and begin mapping. Diviner's data acquisition is reported as ongoing [4]. The Apollo 17 ISR collected about 90 hours of data over five days in lunar orbit [9].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Orbital infrared imagers do not deploy on the surface. They are fixed to the spacecraft, and their viewing is set by spacecraft attitude and, for Diviner, by an articulated elevation/azimuth mount that lets the telescopes view the surface, space and calibration targets [3]. The Apollo 17 ISR was carried on the service module [9]. The LTM's mounting and pointing on Lunar Trailblazer are not described in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 ISR is the earliest example here and flew on the service module during the Apollo 17 mission [9]. Diviner was integrated onto LRO after ground preparation [6][7]. The Lunar Trailblazer LTM was launched as a rideshare payload, but its mission ended in 2025 [11]. ISRO describes IIRS as a Chandrayaan-2 payload [10].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. Compatibility would need the instrument's mass, power, field of view, mounting, thermal and data-interface specifications, which are not publicly specified for these examples in the sources accessed. A surface infrared imager would also need the lander's mechanical, thermal and data interfaces verified.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 ISR demonstrated orbital thermal mapping of the lunar surface. The 1976 contractor report states that its resolution exceeded that of Earth-based measurements by at least an order of magnitude [9]. Diviner is described in the abstract of its 2010 paper, as indexed in search results, as the first instrument to systematically map the global thermal state of the Moon and its diurnal and seasonal variability [1]. Its data continue to be processed and distributed through the PDS [4]. The LTM is an example of a thermal imager carried on a lunar mission that ended before its science operations were reported [11][12]. ISRO describes IIRS as a spectroscopic instrument for composition mapping [10].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
The class definition is broad. The term infrared imager covers broadband radiometers and imaging spectrometers, and the examples are not interchangeable. No single set of values describes the class.
- Apollo 17 ISR: only the 1973 and 1976 abstracts were read for this article, not the full reports [8][9]. Secondary search summaries gave an 80–400 K range and about 30% areal coverage. Neither was confirmed in a primary source, so neither is used.
- Diviner: the EDR SIS, UCLA and PDS pages were read [2][3][4]. The full text of the 2010 paper was not accessible, because the Springer link redirected to a sign-in page [1]. Per-channel spectral ranges are not stated numerically in the pages accessed. The "Diviner Lunar Radar Experiment" wording on the PDS page was treated as a naming error.
- IIRS: ISRO gives band and resolution values [10]. Its operating status, mass and power are not stated there. Early-image reports from October 2019 were found only in secondary news and are not used.
- LTM: channel and resolution values come from eoPortal [11]; the Oxford page gives none [12]. No LTM science data were located in the sources accessed.
- Cross-references: band-specific material belongs to 041 and 042, thermal imaging to 038 and spectral mapping to 035. This article does not duplicate them.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Image URLs were taken from the NASA Photojournal source pages' download links (content-dam JPEG assets), not from search thumbnails or dynamicimage proxy URLs. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Apollo 17 ISR: resolution, accuracy, data-duration and measurement-count values come from the 1976 NASA Contractor Report abstract [9]. The full reports were not read. Secondary search summaries gave an 80–400 K temperature range and about 30% areal coverage; these were not confirmed and are not used. The S-171 designation was not confirmed in a primary source and is not used.

Diviner: mass, power, dimensions and per-channel spectral ranges are not publicly specified in the EDR SIS, UCLA and PDS pages accessed. The full text of the 2010 Space Science Reviews paper was not accessed (the Springer link redirected to a sign-in page); its abstract-level description is from the search-indexed abstract only.
Diviner naming: the PDS Diviner page calls the instrument the 'Diviner Lunar Radar Experiment' while describing a radiometer; the radiometer name is used here and the discrepancy is recorded.

Lunar Thermal Mapper: channel and resolution values rely on the eoPortal summary; the Oxford page gives none. No LTM science data were located. Mass and power are not stated per instrument. Launch date is 27 February 2025 UTC per eoPortal (some entries give 26 February). The Oxford page's 200 kg figure refers to the whole spacecraft.

IIRS: the ISRO payload page gives band and resolution values but no operating status, swath, mass or power. Reports of an October 2019 first illuminated image were found only in secondary news and were not verified against an ISRO primary source; they are not used.

Images: two NASA/JPL Photojournal images were verified (PIA12085 and PIA12088; direct content-dam JPEG URLs returned HTTP 200 image/jpeg on 2026-11-12; identification confirmed on the source pages). Full-resolution TIFF downloads were not checked. No direct image URL was verified for the Apollo 17 ISR, IIRS or LTM, so none is included. The Oxford LTM photograph has only a relative path with a query string and was not used.

Scope: no lunar landing sites are recommended. No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. Cross-references to 035, 038, 041 and 042 are provided rather than duplicating their band-specific content.
